query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of Hf to refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) can improve their high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with a single-phase disordered solid solution structure
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of Hf (less than 1 at.%) to the RHEAs
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (above 800 °C) and loading conditions (tensile or compressive stress)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening and interface strengthening mechanisms
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature mechanical properties (yield strength and ultimate tensile strength) and preserved room-temperature performance (ductility and strength)
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 800-1500 °C, loading conditions: tensile or compressive stress
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Hf required for optimal performance and the potential effects on microstructure and properties at high temperatures

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile tests at high temperatures (800-1500 °C) on RHEAs with and without Hf addition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Hf does not result in improved high-temperature mechanical properties or preserved room-temperature performance, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are considered as a new class of advanced metallic materials, are drawing increasing attention because of their promising properties [,,], such as high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures [,], exceptional ductility [], and toughness []. HEAs were initially defined as alloys containing five or more elements with equal or near-equal concentrations [], while the later studies expended HEAs to include minor elements []. Many studies on HEAs were motivated by the possibility that properties may be tunable based on the elements contained in the HEAs. For example, Al-based HEAs [,,,] were studied for application on aircraft engines and nuclear reactors because of their low densities. On the other hand, because of the high melting temperature and high hardness of W and Re, HEAs that contained W or Re were expected to maintain advanced mechanical properties for high-temperature applications [,].
